extracted.intended_audience: corporate communications professionals, PR practitioners and business leaders
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of high-profile 2023 public relations disasters with lessons for crisis management and reputation strategy. The page extracts practical principles for corporate communications, media relations, governance and stakeholder engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collate, evaluate and escalate information (first rule of crisis management)
rubrics_metrics.description: The BBC initially failed to collate, evaluate and escalate information – the first rule of crisis management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Act quickly to gather available facts, assess their significance and escalate to decision-makers; failure to do so leads to 'playing catch-up' and magnifies reputational harm (example: the Huw Edwards affair).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely reaction and decisive handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Slow to react leaves leadership wrong-footed and playing catch-up; organisations must get a grip quickly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respond promptly to emerging issues to control the narrative and limit escalation. Slow responses (e.g., BBC’s handling of Gary Lineker, OpenAI board ousting) create perceptions of incompetence or confusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistent enforcement of rules and disciplinary standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception that star talent is exempt from rules undermines credibility; organisations must enforce disciplinary standards consistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply policies uniformly across all staff and public figures. Prefer clear, pre-defined standards to ad-hoc exceptions (BBC/Russell Brand and Lineker examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear social media policy and consistent application
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media conduct needs a code and consistent enforcement; patchy application fuels criticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft and apply social media codes of conduct and enforce them visibly. Inconsistent application (e.g., mixed treatment of high-profile presenters) damages trust in leadership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage subject access requests and data disclosure risks
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware the power of the subject access request – it can be used to surface internal communications and embarrass organisations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare for and carefully handle SARs; recognise they can change the dynamics of a dispute or story (NatWest/Coutts briefing example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume no conversation with a journalist is off limits
rubrics_metrics.description: No conversation with a journalist is ever off limits, whether at a charity dinner or in a formal interview setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat all journalist interactions as potentially public; avoid informal briefings that could be quoted or misconstrued. Maintain clear protocols for spokespersons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Succession communications: swift, transparent, positive narrative, stakeholder engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: If you ask ChatGPT about succession planning it gives you three essential phases: Swift and Transparent Communication, Craft a Positive Narrative, and Engage Stakeholders and Manage Expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow those phases in leadership changes: communicate quickly and honestly, shape a forward-looking narrative, and actively involve stakeholders to manage uncertainty (OpenAI/Sam Altman case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use communications to convey security, vision and reset outlook
rubrics_metrics.description: Any opportunity to convey security and vision and take the opportunity to reset the future outlook should be seized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During turmoil, communications should reassure stakeholders, outline a clear plan and reframe the organisation’s future; missed opportunities deepen instability (OpenAI example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative coherence and substantive storytelling beyond image
rubrics_metrics.description: A brand must find a new narrative that does not rely on style or status alone; risk of being perceived as a 'one-trick pony'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop substantive, coherent messaging and avoid relying purely on celebrity/positioning. Superficial PR can be outflanked by stronger institutional narratives (Harry & Meghan example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid procrastination; make timely, principled decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Procrastination gives the impression of fear of making the wrong decision rather than pursuing the right one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide promptly and transparently in sensitive matters; delay can create moral ambiguity and cynicism (Manchester United/Mason Greenwood case).

rubrics_metrics.name: Align crisis responses with stated organisational values
rubrics_metrics.description: An institution's values come to the fore during a crisis — they should be its north star, not a creature of convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure actions match professed values to retain credibility. Opportunistic or inconsistent value application undermines reputational recovery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure robust governance, transparent accounting and management controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Reputation goes beyond media interaction and is closely connected to the structure of an organisation, and how it is governed and managed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain clear governance, financial transparency and oversight to avoid scandals and investigations (Captain Tom Foundation accounting/governance concerns). Weak structures amplify reputational damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listen to and involve external advisors and stakeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: Those outside the central bubble should give advice — if it looks and feels wrong to them, it probably is.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include independent perspectives and heed external counsel; internal echo chambers can miss obvious reputational risks (Captain Tom Foundation interviews and external scrutiny).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantiate environmental and sustainability claims (avoid greenwashing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interrogate every public claim they make and evidence it; misleading imagery or unsupported recyclability/sustainability claims risk regulatory action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document and evidence sustainability statements; avoid suggestive visuals or vague language. Regulators (e.g., CMA) will investigate potential greenwashing (Unilever example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for regulatory, investor and media scrutiny on ESG claims
rubrics_metrics.description: In an environment where the climate emergency is front and centre, increasing scrutiny, legislation and negativity make companies vulnerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect and prepare for detailed challenges from regulators, investors and press; build defensible claims and supply-chain evidence to withstand probes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise humility and pragmatism in corporate climate communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Humility and pragmatism from corporates and the media create an environment that prioritises debate and action versus carbon-related cancel culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid over-claiming ambition or impact; be candid about limitations and practical steps to build credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take decisive leadership action and cultural reform to restore credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Removing leaders and starting over with new leadership to deliver cultural change can be necessary to regain credibility, even if it is risky short-term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider bold structural or leadership changes when problems run deep; accompany them with transparent plans for cultural reform (CBI/Tony Danker example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain coherence and consistency in policy and messaging when rebranding
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy u-turns and inconsistent messaging undermine attempts to rebrand and can damage long-term reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure rebrands are underpinned by consistent policy delivery and realistic commitments; repeated reversals erode public trust (Rishi Sunak/Conservative rebrand example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of optics—perception matters as much as facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The optics of decisions and communications (how things look to the public) have huge reputational impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess not just legal/technical correctness but public perception when making statements or decisions. Poor optics accelerate reputational decline (NatWest share-price hit, various examples).
